stops.name: Arpinum, the villa on the Fibrenus
stops.campa: On the third of January, in the hill country of the Volsci, Marcus Tullius Cicero is born into an equestrian family at the villa where the cold Fibrenus forks around a wooded island before it joins the Liris below Arpinum. He will remember this ground all his life, the plane trees, the little island where he and his brother Quintus will one day walk debating law and the stars. Arpinum gave Rome the soldier Gaius Marius a generation before; it gives Rome now a second son, who will conquer not by the sword but by the tongue.

stops.name: Rome, the Forum — the tirocinium under Scaevola
stops.campa: Cicero takes the toga of manhood and his father brings him to Rome and attaches him to Quintus Mucius Scaevola the augur, the most learned jurist of the age, that he may learn law by standing at his side. He never leaves the old man while he lives, and after his death he attaches himself in the same way to Scaevola the pontifex, his cousin. In the Forum he listens to the consultations of citizens, watches the give and take of the courts, and begins the long apprenticeship of the ear and the tongue that will make him Rome's first voice.

stops.name: The Social War — the camp of Pompeius Strabo
stops.campa: Rome's Italian allies rise in revolt and Cicero, not yet twenty, serves his first campaign in the tent of the consul Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo before Asculum. It is a hard, close war fought against neighbors, and Cicero later says he learned there what war truly costs. In the same camp serves the consul's son, a young man of his own age named Gnaeus Pompeius, called in time Magnus, whose fortune will cross Cicero's own for the rest of both their lives, in the Forum, in the field, and at the last on opposite shores of a civil war.

stops.name: Rome — Philo of Larissa and the arrival of the Academy
stops.campa: Driven from Athens by Mithridates' war, Philo, the head of Plato's own Academy, comes to Rome and opens his lectures to the city. Cicero, seized as he says by an extraordinary zeal for philosophy, gives himself over entirely to him, drinking in the doctrine of the New Academy, that the wise man may argue either side of any question and hold no opinion as certain. It is a habit of mind he never loses: the same suspension of dogma that will let him defend, prosecute, and later meditate every school of Greek thought without ever quite belonging to one.

stops.name: Rome, the Forum — Pro Roscio Amerino
stops.campa: At twenty-six, in Sulla's Rome, Cicero rises to defend Sextus Roscius of Ameria against a charge of parricide brought by men close to the dictator's freedman Chrysogonus, who has already carved up the murdered father's estate among himself. It is a dangerous case and no other advocate will touch it. Cicero wins it, and in doing so quotes old Lucius Cassius, whom the people called the wisest and most honest of judges, who always asked of any crime a single question first.
stops.quote: Cui bono fuerit — to whose benefit was it?

stops.name: Athens — the garden of the Academy
stops.campa: Cicero leaves Rome, giving out that he goes for his health, though friends know Sulla's enmity is not yet spent. He crosses to Athens and sits again under philosophers, this time Antiochus of Ascalon, who is turning the Academy back toward the certainties Philo had loosened. He walks the Academy's own garden, visits the tomb of Plato, and studies with his cousin Lucius and with Atticus, who has made his home in the city and will remain his dearest friend and correspondent for the rest of both their lives.

stops.name: Rhodes — Apollonius Molon and the tears of the Greek master
stops.campa: From Asia, where he hears the rhetors of Adramyttium and Caria and Halicarnassus, Cicero comes at last to Rhodes to study under Apollonius Molon, the reigning master of declamation, and also attends the Stoic Posidonius. Not understanding Latin, Molon asks him to declaim in Greek, so that his faults may be corrected; when he finishes, every listener praises him but Molon sits silent and grave a long while, then speaks the words the school will repeat for centuries after, of admiration for the pupil and pity for the teacher's own exhausted country.

stops.name: Rome — return, marriage to Terentia, the quaestorship won
stops.campa: Two years abroad have changed his voice: the strained, overheated style of the Roscius case has been worked down by exercise and by Molon's discipline into something fuller in the chest and cooler in judgment. He returns to Rome thinner, his health mended, and resumes practice at the bar with a name already made. Terentia, of a well-off family, whom he married about the time he set out, brings a dowry and a will as forceful as his own. Standing for the quaestorship, the first rung of the senatorial ladder, he is elected by every century of the Roman people.

stops.name: Lilybaeum, Sicily — quaestor
stops.campa: Cicero sails to western Sicily as quaestor under the propraetor Sextus Peducaeus, charged with the grain supply out of Lilybaeum in a year of scarcity. He governs so scrupulously, he says, that the Sicilians treat him ever after as their own advocate at Rome. Returning by way of Puteoli, he meets a Roman acquaintance who asks what news from Rome, assuming he means the capital, and is astonished to learn the young man has been abroad on the state's business at all. Cicero takes the lesson to heart: reputation must be renewed at Rome, or Rome forgets it.

stops.name: Syracuse — the forgotten tomb of Archimedes
stops.campa: As quaestor Cicero goes up to Syracuse and asks to see the tomb of Archimedes, dead a hundred and thirty-seven years. The Syracusans know nothing of it and deny any such thing exists. But Cicero remembers a few verses said to be carved there, describing a sphere and a cylinder set upon the stone, and he searches the ground by the Agrigentine Gate until, in a thicket of briars and thorn, he finds a small column rising just above the scrub, bearing the very figures. He orders the brush cut back and stands before the grave the city itself had let vanish.
stops.quote: I remembered certain verses inscribed, as I had heard, on his tomb, and these set forth that a sphere and a cylinder had been put on the top of the grave. So I looked all around, for there are a great quantity of tombs at the Agrigentine Gate, and finally I noted a small column standing out a little above the brambles, on which there was the figure of a sphere and a cylinder.

stops.name: Rome, the Forum — the prosecution of Verres
stops.campa: The Sicilians, remembering their honest quaestor, ask Cicero to prosecute Gaius Verres, their late governor, for three years of extortion, theft of Greek statues and paintings, and the judicial murder of Roman citizens. Verres retains Hortensius, the greatest advocate then living, and counts on delay to run past a friendly jury pool. Cicero breaks the strategy by gathering the evidence himself in Sicily in fifty days and opening with a short, devastating actio prima; Verres does not wait for the second round of speeches but flees to Massilia before Cicero can deliver them, taking his stolen art with him into exile.
stops.quote: Facinus est vincire civem Romanum, scelus verberare, prope parricidium necare: quid dicam in crucem tollere? — It is a crime to bind a Roman citizen, a sin to scourge him, almost an act of parricide to kill him; what shall I say of crucifying him?

stops.name: Tusculum — the villa purchased
stops.campa: With the fees and fame the Verres case brings him, Cicero buys a villa on the slope above the old Latin town of Tusculum, in the hills southeast of Rome, on ground once graced, tradition says, by Sulla himself. Modeled in part on the gymnasia of Athens, it becomes his true home, the place he returns to write, to grieve, and to think, more than any house in the capital. Here in the years ahead he will build his own Academy and Lyceum in miniature, walk the colonnades in argument with his friends, and compose the dialogues that carry Greek philosophy into Latin.
